issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette:
Rangi, a 63-year-old married financial analyst of Oceania background, came to treatment describing how a single life-threatening accident had reorganized his days around danger. Years ago, on his way home, he was caught in a violent crash that left him trapped long enough to believe he might die before help reached him. He remembers the moment with a frightening immediacy: when he tries to tell it, the scene comes back as if it is happening now, not as something finished. The smell inside the vehicle, the dark enclosure around him, and the sharp sounds of cars passing or approaching are not distant reminders to him but forceful keys that unlock the whole event. He can be sitting in his office reviewing figures, hear a vehicle outside the building, and suddenly be back in that instant, hearing the same sounds in his head and feeling as though the danger has returned without warning. The memory does not sit safely in the past for Rangi; it bursts forward with such vividness that it pulls his attention into the old scene and, in turn, makes ordinary smells or darkness feel charged with the same threat.

Since the accident, Rangi has come to believe that he has to be on guard all the time because you never know what can happen next. That conviction shapes how he moves through the world. He scans exits as soon as he enters any room or building, taking stock of doors, hallways, and where he could get out quickly if something went wrong. If he thinks about the accident directly, he becomes convinced he will not be able to handle it, so he pushes the memory away and tries not to dwell on it. Yet the more he tries to keep it at bay, the more easily fragments of it break through. A dark conference room, the smell of exhaust near the parking garage, or the sound of cars pulling up outside his office can bring the full memory back without warning, and once it arrives it feels immediate and impossible to dismiss. Rangi’s own sense that he must stay constantly careful makes the memory more available, while the intrusive memory itself seems to confirm that vigilance is necessary.

What frightened Rangi most was how his body began to react before he had even had time to think. He would wake during the night to check whether he was safe, sometimes sitting up suddenly with his heart racing, needing to look around the bedroom before he could settle. In those moments, he felt certain that if he let his guard down, something terrible could happen again. The same rush of alarm came when the memory returned during the day: his body tensed, his attention narrowed, and he was already in a state of danger before his mind had caught up. This bodily alarm made the memory feel even more present and convincing, as if his reactions proved that the accident was not really over. Once his body was primed like that, the world itself seemed full of possible danger, and he became more alert to smells, darkness, and the approach of cars, noticing them almost instantly and bracing himself before he had a chance to think it through.

Over the months after the accident, Rangi began altering his routines in ways that reached into both home and work. In the office tower where he works as a financial analyst, he avoids lingering in dim corridors and is noticeably uneasy in dark meeting rooms, preferring seats near doors and windows. He notices car sounds in the street below and around the parking area with a start that pulls him out of concentration, and he finds himself monitoring the environment instead of the spreadsheets in front of him. At home, his wife has seen him wake during the night to check the locks and the hall, then listen for sounds outside before returning to bed. He knows these habits are driven by his fear, but he also experiences them as necessary precautions, the only way to stay safe. Even so, the more he remains on guard and the more often he searches for exits or scans for danger, the more readily everyday cues seize him and the more vividly the old scene returns. By the time he sought help, Rangi was exhausted by this cycle and increasingly worried that his life had shrunk to managing threat. He came in hoping to regain some sense that the accident belongs to the past, while admitting that what he fears most is letting his guard down and being caught off guard again.
